title: Seva at your gurdwara
tomorrow: kiran's family isn't sikh. can langar food still be seva for them?

cards: Sunday, 6:40 in the morning. Simran is lacing her shoes for langar dish duty at the gurdwara, her favorite seva: the steam, the stacks of steel plates, the auntie who sings while she scrubs.
Bebe Jaswant blocks the door with one hand. Without a word, she points at the sink. Last night's pots.
Simran's pots. Go on, Bebe says. The Guru's dishes can wait ten minutes.

teach.b: Bebe is passing on an old story. Tradition says that before Amar Das became the third Guru, he served Guru Angad, and every morning before light he carried water from the river for him.

One stormy night, the story goes, he stumbled carrying the pot, and a weaver's wife nearby mocked him as a man with no home. Guru Angad answered by honoring him, and the water-carrier later became Guru.
In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak puts seva right in the middle of ordinary life.

teach.h: SERVE IN THE MIDST OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: In paraphrase: serve in the midst of the world, and you'll be given a place of honor. In the midst of the world. Not only inside the gurdwara.

The Sunday dish line is real seva: cleaning, cooking, minding the shoes, singing kirtan. But the same hands go home. If seva only happens where the sangat can see it, it slowly becomes about being seen.

teach.h: THE POTS NOBODY THANKS YOU FOR.
teach.b: So seva at your gurdwara starts at home, with the pots nobody thanks you for.
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: the water-carrier's seva was plain, and it was daily. Simran scrubs her pots, fast and badly, then slower.
She gets to langar ten minutes late, and the singing auntie hands her a scrubber with a wink.

how: At a gurdwara, volunteers of all ages do seva: cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning, minding shoes at the door and singing kirtan, usually unpaid and unannounced.

games.q: what does “seva at your gurdwara” mean?
o: volunteer hours you log for school credit
selfless service, at the gurdwara and beyond
a fee paid to help keep a gurdwara open

games.q: seva at the gurdwara — tap the pairs.
p: serve in the midst of the world

s: seva only really counts at the gurdwara
Guru Nanak's line puts it in the midst of the world, starting at home.
tradition says Amar Das carried water for Guru Angad before he became Guru
the water-carrier later became the third Guru.
seva at the gurdwara is only cooking and serving food
cleaning, minding shoes and singing kirtan are seva too.

games.q: your cousin does hours of seva at the gurdwara but leaves her room a disaster for her mom to clean. what would Bebe point at?
o: the room: seva in the midst of the world starts at home.
nothing: the gurdwara seva is the kind that really counts.
the gurdwara: she should simply do even more hours there.
games.why: seva in the midst of the world doesn't stop at the gurdwara door. the pots and the room nobody thanks you for are where it starts.

practice: If there's one small thing near you that needs doing, a cup to rinse, a shoe out of place, crumbs on the table, do it now, slowly, the way you would in the Guru's house. Then sit back down and let your hands rest open for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Seva at your gurdwara. Selfless service in the Guru's house: cleaning, cooking, shoes and kirtan, by anyone willing.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service, done without wanting a reward.

carryVoice: Your line: start at home. The pots nobody sees count too, maybe most of all. See you next time.

sources.ref: Ang 26 (Sri Raag, Mahala 1: vich dunia sev kamaaeeai, taa dargah baisan paaeeai), paraphrased
